draft.title: Shrinking distances
card: Distance can be measured in kilometres, but also in the time it takes to get somewhere or send a message. A place can stay the same distance away in kilometres while the time to reach it falls.

Faster transport and faster communication cut that time. Jet aircraft shortened trips that once took weeks by ship to a day or less. Phone and video calls let people talk with someone far away at once.
As these times fall, places feel closer together and the world feels smaller. Geographers call this time-space compression.
Time-space compression changes how far people and businesses can reach in the same amount of time. A trip, a message or an order that once took days can now take hours or seconds.
draft.remember: Time-space compression: less time to reach places, so the world feels smaller.

opts: The time to reach places falls, so the world feels smaller
The kilometres between places shrink as technology improves
Cities grow closer together as more people move into them
Goods become cheaper because they travel shorter distances
a.why: Time-space compression is about the time it takes to travel or communicate falling. The distance in kilometres between places does not change, so the option about kilometres shrinking is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what falls: kilometres or time?

b.q: In the 1850s a letter from Melbourne to London took weeks by sailing ship. Today Mia in Melbourne video calls her cousin in London. Which statement best explains why this is time-space compression?
opts: The time to reach London has fallen, but not the distance
Melbourne has moved closer to London in kilometres
Mia and her cousin now live in the same time zone
Video calls are cheaper than sending letters by ship
b.why: The distance between Melbourne and London is the same, but contact now takes seconds instead of weeks. That fall in time is what makes places feel closer. Cost may also change, but cost is not what time-space compression measures.
b.clue: Ask what has changed: the distance or the time taken?

a.best: The time to reach places falls, so the world feels smaller

b.best: The time to reach London has fallen, but not the distance

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a contrasting qualifier ('but not the distance'). It is also the longest, so it stands out. The clue ('the distance or the time taken?') then narrows the choice further, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.
